subtopic_detail: Choosing between live and recombinant zoster vaccine in a patient on immunosuppression
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62 year old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis in remission on methotrexate 20 mg weekly by subcutaneous injection and prednisolone 5 mg daily. Her neighbour has just had a painful rash across one side of the chest and she asks whether she can be protected against the same thing.

She has never had shingles and has no history of chickenpox vaccination. She has no active infection, her arthritis has been quiet for two years and she has no plans to change her treatment.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and creatinine within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Methotrexate 20 mg weekly subcutaneously, folic acid 5 mg weekly, prednisolone 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to shingles prevention?

options.text: Give the live attenuated zoster vaccine at today's consultation
options.rationale: Live attenuated zoster vaccine is contraindicated in significant immunosuppression because the attenuated virus can disseminate, and methotrexate at this dose with daily prednisolone meets that threshold (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Give the recombinant zoster vaccine as two doses two months apart
options.rationale: The recombinant subunit vaccine contains no live virus, is the preferred product in immunocompromised adults, and is given as two doses with a minimum interval of one to two months in this group (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Give the live attenuated vaccine four weeks after stopping methotrexate
options.rationale: Interrupting effective disease modifying therapy risks a flare, and a four week washout is insufficient because immune reconstitution after methotrexate and corticosteroid is not assured in that period (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook; Australian Rheumatology Association).

options.text: Advise that no zoster vaccine can be given while she is immunosuppressed
options.rationale: This confuses the contraindication that applies only to the live product with a blanket rule, and it withholds protection from precisely the group at highest risk of severe zoster and postherpetic neuralgia (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Prescribe valaciclovir 500 mg daily as long term shingles prophylaxis
options.rationale: Continuous antiviral prophylaxis is used around haematopoietic stem cell transplantation rather than for routine rheumatological immunosuppression, and it does not generate the durable cellular immunity a vaccine provides (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Herpes zoster reactivates when varicella specific cell mediated immunity wanes, so the people most likely to need protection are often the people in whom a live vaccine is unsafe. The recombinant subunit vaccine solved this problem because it contains glycoprotein E with an adjuvant and no replicating virus, giving efficacy above 90 per cent that is preserved in immunocompromised adults. In Australia it is funded on the National Immunisation Program for adults from 65 years of age, for First Nations adults from 50 years of age, and for immunocompromised people from 18 years of age under defined conditions. Reactogenicity is high, with fever and marked injection site pain common for a day or two, and patients should be warned so they return for the second dose.
key_points: Live attenuated zoster vaccine is contraindicated in significant immunosuppression
The recombinant subunit vaccine contains no live virus and is safe in this group
Two doses are required, with a shortened minimum interval in immunocompromised adults
Efficacy remains above 90 per cent in older and immunocompromised adults
Warn patients about marked reactogenicity so they complete the second dose
explanation.pearls: In immunocompromised adults the second dose of recombinant zoster vaccine may be brought forward to one to two months after the first rather than the usual two to six months, so that protection is complete before further immunosuppression is escalated.

subtopic_detail: Applying direct oral anticoagulant dose reduction criteria in a small older patient
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing an 84 year old woman admitted with a chest infection in whom an irregularly irregular pulse was noted. Her electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation at 88 beats per minute with no acute ischaemic change, which she had not noticed herself.

She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes and takes aspirin 100 mg daily, which was started years ago after a fall. She has had no bleeding and no falls in the past year, and she manages her own medicines with a dose administration aid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute and irregular, blood pressure 138/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 121 micromol/L (45-90), calculated creatinine clearance 28 mL/min, haemoglobin 124 g/L (120-160), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antithrombotic regimen?

options.text: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily with six monthly renal function testing
options.rationale: She meets two of the three reduction criteria of age 80 years or more, weight 60 kg or less and creatinine 133 micromol/L or more, so the reduced dose applies, and apixaban is the only direct oral anticoagulant with an Australian dose for a creatinine clearance in the high twenties (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily with six monthly renal function testing
options.rationale: The full dose applies only when fewer than two reduction criteria are met, and she satisfies both the age and the weight criterion (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily with six monthly renal function testing
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban is reduced to 15 mg daily once creatinine clearance falls below 50 mL per minute, so the 20 mg dose would be an overdose at a clearance of 28 mL per minute (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily with six monthly renal function testing
options.rationale: Dabigatran is the most renally cleared of the direct oral anticoagulants at around 80 per cent and is contraindicated below a creatinine clearance of 30 mL per minute (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily with six monthly cardiovascular risk assessment
options.rationale: Aspirin gives negligible stroke protection in atrial fibrillation while retaining much of the bleeding risk, and it is no longer recommended as an alternative to anticoagulation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

explanation.summary: Newly detected atrial fibrillation during an acute illness still warrants stroke risk assessment, because most of these patients have paroxysmal atrial fibrillation that persists after the illness resolves. Australian practice uses the CHA2DS2-VA score, which drops the sex category, and recommends anticoagulation at a score of two or more. The commonest prescribing error in this population is failing to apply dose reduction criteria in small older patients, which more than doubles bleeding risk, and the second commonest is choosing an agent whose renal clearance makes it unsafe. Renal function should be rechecked at least six monthly, and more often during intercurrent illness, because a falling clearance can move a patient across a dosing threshold.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA of two or more warrants anticoagulation in Australian practice
Apixaban is reduced when two of age, weight and creatinine criteria are met
Dabigatran is contraindicated below a creatinine clearance of 30 mL per minute
Rivaroxaban is reduced to 15 mg daily below a clearance of 50 mL per minute
Aspirin is not an acceptable substitute for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation
explanation.pearls: The apixaban reduction criteria are age 80 years or more, weight 60 kg or less and serum creatinine 133 micromol per litre or more, and any two of the three trigger 2.5 mg twice daily regardless of the calculated creatinine clearance.

subtopic_detail: Acting on out of office blood pressure when clinic readings disagree
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 47 year old teacher whose blood pressure has been recorded above target at three separate visits over the past two months. He feels well, exercises twice a week, drinks four standard drinks a week and has never smoked.

He tells you he gets tense in medical rooms and that a machine at the pharmacy gave him much lower numbers. He has no headaches, no snoring, no palpitations and no family history of early cardiovascular disease. His fundi show no arteriolar narrowing or haemorrhage.

data_table.Vital signs: Clinic blood pressure readings of 156/96, 152/94 and 158/98 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 92 mL/min/1.73m2, urine albumin to creatinine ratio 1.4 mg/mmol (less than 2.5), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), fasting lipids and glucose within normal limits
data_table.Ambulatory monitoring: Daytime average 128/78 mmHg, night time average 110/66 mmHg, 24 hour average 124/74 mmHg
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with no left ventricular hypertrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start perindopril 5 mg daily and review the blood pressure in six weeks
options.rationale: Treating on clinic readings alone in this situation exposes a normotensive man to drug adverse effects and to symptomatic hypotension outside the consulting room (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline).
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

options.text: Start amlodipine 5 mg daily and review the blood pressure in six weeks
options.rationale: Changing the drug class does not change the underlying problem, which is that the out of office average is below the diagnostic threshold and there is no target organ damage (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline).
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

options.text: Refer for investigation of a secondary cause of the raised readings
options.rationale: Secondary hypertension is pursued when hypertension is confirmed and is resistant, of early onset, or accompanied by suggestive features such as hypokalaemia, none of which apply here (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline).
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

options.text: Give lifestyle advice and repeat ambulatory monitoring in twelve months
options.rationale: A daytime ambulatory average below 135/85 mmHg with normal renal, cardiac and retinal assessment defines the white coat pattern, which is managed with lifestyle measures and periodic repeat monitoring because a proportion progress to sustained hypertension (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline).
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

options.text: Treat according to the clinic readings and add a second agent if needed
options.rationale: Escalating on clinic readings compounds the original error and is the mechanism by which patients with this pattern accumulate three or more unnecessary antihypertensive drugs (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline).
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

explanation.summary: Australian guidance treats out of office measurement as the reference standard for diagnosing hypertension because clinic readings misclassify a substantial minority of patients in both directions. The diagnostic thresholds are lower out of office, with a daytime ambulatory or home average of 135/85 mmHg corresponding to a clinic reading of 140/90 mmHg, and a 24 hour average threshold of 130/80 mmHg. The white coat pattern carries a cardiovascular risk intermediate between normotension and sustained hypertension, so it is followed rather than ignored. The mirror image, masked hypertension, has normal clinic readings with a raised out of office average and carries risk equivalent to sustained hypertension, which is why ambulatory monitoring is also indicated when target organ damage appears despite normal clinic readings.
key_points: Out of office measurement is the reference standard for diagnosing hypertension
Daytime ambulatory threshold is 135/85 mmHg, not the clinic threshold of 140/90 mmHg
The white coat pattern needs surveillance rather than drug treatment
Assess target organ damage before deciding, using renal, cardiac and retinal findings
Masked hypertension carries risk equivalent to sustained hypertension
explanation.pearls: A nocturnal fall in blood pressure of less than 10 per cent identifies a non dipping pattern that independently predicts cardiovascular events, so read the night time average on every ambulatory report rather than only the daytime figure.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

subtopic_detail: Recognising dopaminergic augmentation rather than disease progression in restless legs syndrome
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 62 year old man who has taken pramipexole for restless legs syndrome for three years. The dose has been increased twice because his symptoms kept breaking through, and each increase helped for a few months.

He now says the crawling feeling starts in the middle of the afternoon rather than at bedtime, and that in the past six months it has begun to affect his arms as well as his legs. He has no numbness, his ankle reflexes are present and his pedal pulses are normal. He takes no antihistamine, antidepressant or antiemetic.

data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 190 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 32 per cent (15-45), creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate within normal limits, haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180)
data_table.Medications: Pramipexole 0.75 mg at night, increased from 0.25 mg over three years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase pramipexole and add a bedtime dose to cover the afternoon
options.rationale: Escalating the dopamine agonist is the specific trap here, because each increase drives further augmentation and produces earlier and more widespread symptoms within months (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Add oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily and reassess in three months
options.rationale: Iron replacement is first line when ferritin is below 75 micrograms per litre or transferrin saturation below 20 per cent, and neither threshold is crossed here so iron will not help (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Taper and cease pramipexole and commence gabapentin at night
options.rationale: Earlier onset of symptoms in the day, spread to the arms and loss of response to each dose increase define augmentation, which is managed by withdrawing the dopamine agonist slowly and substituting an alpha 2 delta ligand such as gabapentin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Change to a rotigotine patch and continue the current evening dose
options.rationale: Rotigotine is another dopamine agonist and although its continuous delivery causes augmentation less often, switching within the same class while continuing the oral drug perpetuates the problem (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Add clonazepam 0.5 mg at night and continue pramipexole unchanged
options.rationale: A benzodiazepine may improve sleep continuity but does nothing for the daytime urge to move, and adding it in an older man risks falls and daytime sedation (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Augmentation is the paradoxical worsening of restless legs syndrome caused by long term dopaminergic therapy and affects a substantial proportion of patients treated with dopamine agonists for several years. It is recognised by symptoms starting earlier in the day, spreading to previously unaffected body parts, becoming more intense, and by a shorter latency at rest, with each dose increase producing only temporary relief. It is frequently misread as progression of the underlying disorder, and the resulting dose escalation accelerates the process. Withdrawal is uncomfortable and should be gradual, with an alpha 2 delta ligand introduced before the taper begins, and iron studies repeated because low brain iron lowers the threshold for augmentation even when the ferritin is not frankly low.
key_points: Augmentation means earlier onset, greater intensity and spread to new body regions
Each dose increase gives only temporary relief and worsens the underlying process
Alpha 2 delta ligands such as gabapentin or pregabalin do not cause augmentation
Withdraw the dopamine agonist gradually because rebound symptoms are severe
Check ferritin and transferrin saturation before attributing symptoms to augmentation
explanation.pearls: In restless legs syndrome the iron treatment threshold is a ferritin below 75 micrograms per litre or a transferrin saturation below 20 per cent, which is far higher than the threshold used to diagnose iron deficiency anaemia.

subtopic_detail: Formed visual hallucinations with retained insight in a patient with severe visual loss
stem:
You are the general practitioner making a home visit to an 81 year old woman with advanced age related macular degeneration whose corrected acuity is 6/60 in both eyes. For three months she has seen small figures in old fashioned clothing standing near her armchair, and repeating brick patterns across her lounge room wall, several times a day for a few minutes at a time.

She tells you she knows they cannot really be there and finds them more puzzling than frightening. She hears no voices, smells nothing unusual and holds no unusual beliefs. She sleeps well, has started no new medicines, and her daughter says her memory and conversation are unchanged.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid stimulating hormone and urinalysis within normal limits
data_table.Cognitive assessment: Mini Mental State Examination 28 out of 30, with points lost on the copying task

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence risperidone 0.5 mg at night and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are ineffective for this syndrome because the hallucinations arise from deafferented visual cortex rather than dopaminergic overactivity, and they add falls, stroke and mortality risk in an older woman (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence quetiapine 25 mg at night and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Choosing a lower potency antipsychotic does not change the fact that no drug is indicated, and sedation in an older person with poor vision compounds the risk of falls (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence donepezil 5 mg daily and arrange cognitive assessment
options.rationale: The near pair is dementia with Lewy bodies, where visual hallucinations occur with fluctuating cognition, parkinsonism and dream enactment, none of which are present in a woman whose cognition and conversation are unchanged (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain and admit
options.rationale: Urgent imaging is warranted when hallucinations accompany focal signs, headache, seizure or a fluctuating conscious state, and a three month history with normal cognition and normal bloods does not meet that bar (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Explain the condition, improve lighting and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Formed visual hallucinations with full insight, no other hallucinatory modality and no delusions in a person with severe visual loss is Charles Bonnet syndrome, and explanation plus optimising lighting and visual stimulation is the treatment (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists; Vision Australia).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Charles Bonnet syndrome describes complex visual hallucinations in people with acquired visual impairment who have intact cognition and retained insight. The mechanism is release phenomenon in visual association cortex deprived of input, analogous to musical hallucinations in acquired deafness, and the images are typically people, faces, patterns or landscapes seen in the affected visual field. It is common, affecting perhaps one in eight people with significant macular disease, and it is grossly underreported because patients fear being thought to have a mental illness. Explanation itself is therapeutic, and most cases settle over 12 to 18 months as visual loss stabilises or the brain adapts, so drug treatment is rarely required.
key_points: Retained insight and absence of other hallucinatory modalities are the defining features
It occurs with any cause of visual loss, not only macular degeneration
The equivalent phenomenon in acquired deafness is musical hallucination
Explanation and reassurance are the main treatment and relieve considerable distress
Antipsychotics are ineffective and carry substantial risk in this population
explanation.pearls: Increasing ambient lighting, blinking or shifting gaze can abort an episode within seconds, and telling the patient this specific manoeuvre gives them control and reduces distress more reliably than any drug.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
